slides.title: Homogeneous Spaces
slides.notes: Open by making the quotient picture concrete. A homogeneous space is a geometry whose points are all reached from one chosen origin by a symmetry group. The chapter asks which connection, metric, holonomy, and complex-structure questions can be answered by inspecting Lie algebra data at that origin.

slides.title: Six Lenses For Reading The Source Span
slides.notes: Use this route slide to keep the chapter from becoming a catalogue of propositions. Each section reduces a geometric question to data at the base point. The repeated teaching move is to ask what remains after symmetry has removed all irrelevant pointwise variation.

slides.title: A Point Is A Coset, And Symmetry Moves It
slides.notes: Emphasize that the quotient notation is not decorative. It tells students where all local data can be stored: at the coset H, modulo the directions that only move inside the stabilizer. This is the reason later connection and metric conditions become algebraic compatibility tests.

slides.title: Frames Carry The Symmetry Upstairs
slides.notes: This slide connects the chapter to the principal bundle language from earlier chapters. Students should see that a G-structure is a controlled set of frames, not a new kind of point. Symmetry upstairs is the bookkeeping device that makes invariant connection data well-defined.

slides.title: Wang Data Replaces A Moving Connection Form
slides.notes: Present Wang's correspondence as the main compression theorem for the first section. The map A is not arbitrary: on isotropy directions it must reproduce the isotropy representation, and under H it must transform equivariantly. These two rules are the price of encoding a global connection at one point.

slides.title: The Same Linear Map Controls Covariant Differentiation
slides.notes: The goal here is to prevent A from feeling like an abstract artifact. It tells how a symmetry-generated vector field differs from the covariant derivative chosen by the connection. This difference becomes the practical bridge to torsion, curvature, and later holonomy calculations.

slides.title: A Complement m Becomes The Model Tangent Space
slides.notes: Spend time on the word reductive because it does much of the chapter's work. The complement m is not merely a vector-space convenience. Its invariance under isotropy means that algebra performed in m remains meaningful after changing the representative of the base frame.

slides.title: The Zero m-Map Choice Exposes Bracket Geometry
slides.notes: Connect the picture to the formulas slowly. In the canonical connection, m is declared horizontal, so the bracket of two m-directions is the experiment. The m-component contributes torsion, while the h-component rotates frames through the isotropy representation and contributes curvature.

slides.title: Invariant Tensors Become Origin-Level Checks
slides.notes: Make the classroom payoff explicit. If a tensor is invariant, students do not need to check it point by point. They can inspect its value at the origin and the isotropy action. The canonical connection then upgrades this invariance into parallelism for reductive homogeneous spaces.

slides.title: A Symmetric Correction Keeps The Canonical Geodesies
slides.notes: This is a good place to slow down because names can mislead. The canonical connection is not automatically torsion-free. The natural torsion-free connection is chosen to preserve the canonical geodesic family, while later metric compatibility may impose a different or coincident choice.

slides.title: A Metric Is A Bilinear Form That Survives Isotropy
slides.notes: The invariant metric result should feel parallel to the invariant tensor result. A metric is determined by one bilinear form at the origin, but that form must be insensitive to the isotropy action. This provides a concrete algebraic test for whether a proposed metric descends to K/H.

slides.title: Levi-Civita Data Adds A Symmetric Correction
slides.notes: Use this slide to show how the Riemannian connection is still algebraic on a reductive homogeneous space. The bracket gives the skew part, but metric compatibility and zero torsion require the symmetric term U. Naturally reductive spaces are special because this extra correction vanishes.

slides.title: Curvature Simplifies When The Metric And Bracket Cooperate
slides.notes: This slide should give students a reason to care about the naturally reductive condition. It is not just a naming convention; it says the symmetry orbits are compatible with the Riemannian geodesic structure. That compatibility makes curvature and decomposition statements easier to read from Lie algebra data.

slides.title: Curvature Starts The Algebra, Stability Closes It
slides.notes: Frame holonomy as an algorithm. Curvature supplies the first infinitesimal rotations, but those rotations must be closed under the connection's own infinitesimal transport. The theorem's smallest subalgebra language is exactly this iterative closure process, specialized to invariant data.

slides.title: A Normal Invariant Connection Makes The Holonomy Bundle Visible
slides.notes: Use this picture to make the holonomy bundle less mysterious. It is not chosen by hand; it is the subset of frames that horizontal motion can actually reach. Normality says the symmetry group K still sees this smaller bundle transitively, so invariant and parallel behavior become tightly linked.

slides.title: Homogeneity Organizes The Product Factors
slides.notes: The de Rham section answers a structural question. If the metric geometry splits into factors, homogeneity should not disappear from the pieces. Students should connect this with holonomy: invariant subspaces and irreducible factors are detected by how the holonomy and isotropy actions preserve tangent decompositions.

slides.title: Integrability Becomes An Algebraic Bracket Test
slides.notes: Close the mathematical arc by showing that complex geometry also follows the same pattern. An invariant almost complex structure is first a linear operator at the origin that squares to minus identity and respects isotropy. Integrability then asks whether the Lie bracket obstruction vanishes.

slides.title: What Students Should Be Able To Do After This Lecture
slides.notes: End with active recall rather than a long list of theorems. Ask students to explain one invariant object, name the algebraic compatibility condition that defines it, and describe a failure mode. That exercise reveals whether they understand the chapter's central method rather than only its vocabulary.
